newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq presses button to resume oil exports.
newsitem.headline: Iraq presses button to resume oil exports.

text.p: Iraqi President Saddam Hussein pressed the button that resumed Iraqi oil exports to world markets on Tuesday after a six-year break, the official Iraqi News Agency reported.

"President Saddam Hussein pressed the button in Kirkuk's Number One pumping station at 11.25 Baghdad time (0825 GMT), declaring the return of Iraqi oil to the international market," the agency reported from Kirkuk in northern Iraq.
Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said earlier in a statement that Iraq would pump 650,000 barrels on Tuesday from Kirkuk through its pipeline to Turkey.

The United Nations gave Iraq clearance on Monday to start resuming limited exports from Tuesday under an "oil-for-food" deal to buy humanitarian aid for Iraqis suffering under economic sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Iraqis celebrated in the streets of Baghdad on Monday night, firing guns into the air and singing and dancing, residents said.
Rasheed said that Iraq had sent two contracts to the U.N. Secretary-General that would enable Iraq to sell its oil to international companies. The statement did not name the purchasers.
"Iraq will export today (Tuesday) 650,000 barrels of crude oil through the Turkish port of Ceyhan," Rasheed said in a statement carried by the official Iraqi News Agency.
Rasheed said Iraq would give preference to Turkey in selling its oil.
Oil from Iraq's southern terminal of Mina al-Bakr would start to flow on Friday or Saturday, Rasheed added.

Under the U.N. plan, concluded in May but held up by disputes over implementation, Iraq will be able to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods.
Security Council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy called it "the largest humanitarian operation ever launched by the United Nations in the world."

Speaking to reporters in New York after notifying council members that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali had given the final go-ahead, Fulci said: "More than 20 million innocent Iraqi civilians will be finally saved from starvation and untold suffering."
"It means that anaesthesia will finally be available for surgery. It also means that four out of 10 newborn children will no longer die before they reach age one," Fulci said.
Both the oil sales and the purchase of humanitarian supplies are subject to close U.N. monitoring. If all goes well, the Security Council may renew the deal when the initial six months expire.

In Washington, State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies stressed that the agreement did "not signal an end or the first step toward the end of the sanctions regime against Iraq, against (President) Saddam Hussein's regime."

A prime condition for the full lifting of sanctions, which includes a ban on normal oil sales, is word from the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of disarming Iraq that all its weapons of mass destruction have been scrapped.
The head of the commission, ambassador Rolf Ekeus, is on one of his periodic visits to Baghdad, trying to account for Iraq's arsenal of SCUD missiles.
Traders and shipping sources said in Europe on Monday that it was highly unlikely Iraqi oil would hit the market for at least a couple of weeks, at the soonest.
Spokesmen for France's Elf Aquitaine and Total, two of the first companies expected to be awarded contracts, said on Monday their firms had not signed deals yet.

In giving the green light, Boutros-Ghali said: "This is a victory for the poorest of the poor of Iraq, for the women, the children, the sick and the disabled. I hope the humanitarian dimension will always prevail in the work of the United Nations."

The U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) has said 4,500 children under the age of five were dying each month from hunger and disease while the U.N. World Food Programme estimated about 180,000 children under five were malnourished.
